title: A small bulge. A possible clue.
subtitle: A close-up of what might happen behind a wooden face.
summary: Open a low drain in a cloth-lined mold. Water escapes, the fabric bows outward, and the retained material leaves a protrusion when it hardens.
sceneDescription: A cutaway timber mold holding granular stone mixture. Cloth bulges through a low opening while blue water droplets drain into a small pool.
modelNote: A qualitative cutaway of a proposed mechanism. Drainage and bulging are animated, not predictions from a fluid or fabric simulation.

steps.name: Fill
steps.title: Hold the wet mixture in a lined form.
steps.text: A cloth lining separates the illustrated mineral mixture from the timber facing. The front is cut away so the proposed mechanism can be seen.

steps.name: Open
steps.title: Give excess water an outlet.
steps.text: A low opening exposes the cloth. Toggle the drain to compare the pictured sequence with a closed form.

steps.name: Drain
steps.title: Water passes. Solids stay behind.
steps.text: The illustration assumes a permeable fabric that retains the particles. Pressure bows it into the opening and carries some mixture outward.

steps.name: Harden
steps.title: The bulge becomes part of the block.
steps.text: If the material hardens while the cloth remains bowed, the protrusion can survive removal of the mold.

steps.name: Reveal
steps.title: A construction detail leaves a trace.
steps.text: A nub remains in the open-drain scenario. The closed-drain view is a geometric comparison; it does not assert how either real mixture would cure.

issues.title: Protrusions left on a finished face
issues.mechanism: A cloth-covered outlet offers a way for a nub to form as part of the block, without carving the whole face back around it.
issues.remaining: This still needs a physical replication that matches the shape, texture, and internal continuity of a particular ancient nub.

issues.title: Why only some blocks?
issues.mechanism: A selective-drain scenario would add an outlet only where the mix needed drainage.
issues.remaining: Selective drainage is an extension explored here, not a demonstrated historical practice or a claim that all casting recipes need drains.

hypothesis: Fóti proposes a fabric-drainage origin for some stone protrusions. This study isolates the geometry and adds a selectable drain; it does not assume that every nub has the same origin.
alternative: Bosses left during dressing, handling features, and unfinished surfaces offer other explanations. Their relevance depends on the individual stone and construction context.
test: Cast matched specimens with a closed form, an open hole, and a cloth-covered hole. Record water loss, fabric deflection, curing, and nub shape. Compare internal structure and surface weave with documented examples.
